name: The Florence Court Irish Yew

location.address: Florence Court, Rourkefield Road, Florencecourt, Enniskillen BT92 1DJ

story:
Every Irish yew standing in a churchyard anywhere is said to be a cutting of this one, and it is not much to look at. The botanists who know it best say it survives rather than thrives. It is low, scraggy and lichen-covered, cut back for two centuries of cuttings and shaded for years by ash and sycamore.

It began as a wild plant. A farmer called George Willis found two upright yew seedlings on the slopes of Cuilcagh, at a rock known as Carraig-na-madadh, the Rock of the Dog, and gave one to his landlord, Lord Mountflorence, later Earl of Enniskillen. Of the two, only this one lives. When that happened is argued over. Sources give 1740, 1760, 1764, 1767 and 1780, and the Fermanagh botanists put the collecting before 1767, perhaps as early as 1740. That makes the planted tree at least about 250 years old, and the wild seedling older still.

Clearing and pruning in 1980 helped it, and in 2010 it was reported stable, with moss slowing its growth. That is also the last dated report on its condition we could read, so if you have seen it recently, tell us how it looks.

It stands beside a small stream in a glade at Florence Court, a National Trust estate with paid entry for non-members. Storm Eowyn damaged Northern Ireland's estates in January 2025, so check the Trust's page first.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by how unimpressive it is, a low, scraggy, misshapen yew rather than a tall column. It stands beside a small stream in a glade at Florence Court, sheltered by laurels and taller trees.
access: Paid entry: National Trust property (Florence Court); members free, non-members pay admission, current price and hours on the National Trust site (not fetched, NT site blocked us). The tree stands in a stream-side glade in the demesne, reached on foot from the house grounds. Check the NT page before travelling: Storm Eowyn (Jan 2025) damaged NI Trust estates.
transport: No public transport worth naming; about 12 km (15 min drive) south-west of Enniskillen, Fermanagh. Ulsterbus rural services are infrequent.
pin_source: OSM natural=tree node 5274376196 named 'Florence Court Irish Yew' (54.2541069, -7.7229609); Wikipedia coordinate 54.2542, -7.7231 agrees within 15 m.
recognise_facts: Not a tall column: a low, scraggy, misshapen yew beside a small stream in a glade, sheltered by laurels and taller trees. It is the mother of all Irish yews, which is why it is the one visitors ask for.
verify_notes: Sources: Wikipedia (Florence Court Yew; custodian National Trust; date seeded 1767; two seedlings, one died, this one survives; heavy cutting and shade from ash and sycamore; 'stable' as of 2010 with moss slowing growth); BSBI Fermanagh account (original plants collected as juveniles before 1767, possibly as early as 1740; found by George Willis, farmer at Aghatirourke, Killesher parish, on the NE slopes of Cuilcagh at Carraig-na-madadh, 'The Rock of the Dog'; gave the second plant to his landlord Lord Mountflorence, later Earl of Enniskillen; the tree 'survives rather than thrives', scraggy, overgrown with lichens; clearing and pruning in 1980 helped; grows beside a small stream in a glade sheltered by laurels, on land BSBI says is managed by NI Forest Service). Dates conflict by source: 1740 / 1760 / 1764 / 1767 / 1780 appear; BSBI first record at Florencecourt by J.T. Mackay 1825. All Irish yews are said to descend from cuttings of this tree (Wikipedia: oldest Irish yew alive). Age: tree is a clone of a wild seedling taken before 1767; the planted tree is therefore at least about 250 years old, wild seedling older. Height 7.5 m is from search-summary only, NOT a seen figure; do not use. Girth not found. Flagged: single dated condition report is 2010 (Wikipedia); a search summary says the tree was selected for the Queen's Green Canopy in 2022 (Fermanagh Herald, page 403 to us, unseen). iNaturalist observation within 100 m region 2025-10-12 (weak area-level life check). Hosts: nationaltrust.org.uk (Radware challenge), fermanaghherald.com (403).

name: The Crom Yews

location.address: Old Crom Castle ruins, Crom Estate, Newtownbutler, Fermanagh BT92 8AJ

story:
Two yews at Crom are said to have marked the entrance to a castle garden that has not existed since the 1760s. The old castle was built in 1611, during the Plantation of Ulster, and burnt in the early 1760s. Today they stand at the ruins on the Crom estate, on Upper Lough Erne, and the garden they once flanked is gone.

Nobody knows how old they are, and the claims are wide. Lord Erne is said to put them at 800 years. A National Trust trail guide, by a summary we could not read in full, gives anything from 400 to 1,000, and the Trust itself admits the debate has run for years. We leave the age open. The earliest written mention we found is J.C. Loudon's, in 1837.

The numbers that are on record come from the Tree Register of Ireland in 2000. The larger yew measured 474 cm round, taken low at 10 cm above the ground, and 10.8 metres tall. Its partner was 430 cm round and taller, at 14 metres. Photographs show branches that have rooted where they touch the ground. We found no measurement since, so treat these as figures from that 2000 record.

Crom is a National Trust estate with paid entry for non-members. Some of its trees are so old that access to them is restricted, so look from the path. Hours differ between listings and Storm Eowyn changed some routes in 2025, so check first.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the pair of big yews at the ruins of Old Crom Castle, said to mark the old garden entrance. The larger is 474 cm round near the ground, the smaller 430 cm; our pin is approximate.

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database (from Tree Register of Ireland 2000), Crom Castle 2084 and 2085

access: Paid entry: National Trust Crom Estate (members free; non-members pay, price on the NT site, not fetched). Estate open to the public per Wikipedia; the same page says some trees are so ancient that physical access is restricted, so view from the path. Opening hours differ between listings: confirm on the NT page. Storm Eowyn (Jan 2025) changed some routes.
transport: No useful public transport; about 5 km from Newtownbutler, about 25 km south-east of Enniskillen by road.

location_site.name: Old Crom Castle ruins garden entrance

recognise_facts: Two big yews at the ruins of Old Crom Castle (built 1611, burnt 1764), said to mark the original entrance to the old castle garden. The larger has a 474 cm girth, the smaller 430 cm.
verify_notes: Ancient Yew Group (citing Tree Register of Ireland 2000): two yews at Crom Castle. ID 2084 larger: girth 474 cm at 10 cm above ground, height 10.8 m, earliest mention 1837 (J.C. Loudon), category 'Ancient 4-5 m'; ID 2085 the lesser-girthed: 430 cm at 10 cm, height 14 m. Wikipedia Crom Estate: old castle built 1611 in the Plantation of Ulster, burnt early 1760s; estate given to National Trust by 6th Earl of Erne 1987; some trees so ancient physical access is restricted. name: The Dark Hedges

location.address: Bregagh Road, Armoy, Ballymoney BT53 8TU (between Ballinlea Road and Ballykenver Road)

story:
The road through the Dark Hedges has been closed to traffic since 2017, to protect the beeches that made it famous. The Stuart family planted about 150 beeches around 1775 along the entrance drive to Gracehill House, and over two and a half centuries their crowns grew together into a tunnel over the Bregagh Road. Then Game of Thrones filmed it as the King's Road, and the coaches came.

The tunnel is thinning. Since 2016 storms have taken beeches almost every year. Gertrude took them in 2016, Doris in 2017, Hector in 2018, an unnamed gale in 2019, Arwen in 2021, three in Isha in 2024 and two more in Eowyn in January 2025. Others have been felled for safety. The count of survivors is not settled. A 2023 survey reported 86, and a more recent tally says around 75, so somewhere between the two is the honest answer. Nobody says 150 remain.

The trees have had a preservation order since 2004 and a trust of their own since 2009. On 30 October 2017 the road between Ballinlea Road and Ballykenver Road was closed to all but emergency and farm vehicles, partly because of the storm losses and the weight of traffic. You walk it now.

The beeches stand on private land beside the public road. Look from the road and stay out of the fields. Parking is at the Ballinlea Road end, and the road itself is sometimes closed to walkers too while tree work goes on.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the tunnel of interlaced beeches arching over the narrow Bregagh Road, the old drive to Gracehill House. Stand on the road and look along it; the trees are on private land either side.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the tunnel turns copper and russet overhead

access: Free. Public road, closed to general vehicles (traffic ban on Bregagh Road between Ballinlea Road and Ballykenver Road since 30 October 2017; emergency and agricultural vehicles exempt), so it is walked. The beeches stand on privately owned land beside the road: look from the road, do not enter the fields. Pedestrian closures happen for tree-safety works (Nov 2023). Parking at the Ballinlea Road end (OSM 'Dark Hedges Parking').
transport: No bus to the door; about 3 km from Armoy village, 15 km from Ballymoney, on the Causeway Coast; Translink rural services to Armoy are infrequent. Many visitors come by car or coach tour.
pin_source: OSM tourism=viewpoint node 2393737678 'The Dark Hedges' (55.135169, -6.381941); Wikipedia 55.1344, -6.3806; OSM tree_row way 441798399 spans 55.1328..55.1366. Pin is the viewing point at the avenue, one place to stand.
recognise_facts: A tunnel of interlaced beeches arching over a narrow road, planted along the old entrance drive to Gracehill House. The ensemble is the destination; stand on the road and look along it.
verify_notes: Ensemble entry, one place to stand (the avenue); alive trees only. Wikipedia: planted around 1775 by the Stuart family along the entrance road to Gracehill House (built by James Stuart); about 150 originally; about 90 by 2016; a 2023 survey counted 86 with 11 in poor condition and 6 felled for safety (Irish Times 20 Nov 2023, search listing); Wikipedia lead says 'around 75' remain as of 2026 and does not reconcile with the 86. Irish News (Jan 2024): Storm Isha felled three, the Dark Hedges Preservation Trust chair Mervyn Storey; article cites roughly 150 originally; trees on privately owned land near Stranocum. STORM LOSSES per Wikipedia: Gertrude Jan 2016 (2 destroyed, 1 damaged), Doris Feb 2017 (1), Hector Jun 2018 (1), unnamed Jan 2019 (1), Arwen 27 Nov 2021 (2), Isha Jan 2024 (3), Eowyn 24 Jan 2025 (2). Tree preservation order 2004; Dark Hedges Preservation Trust founded 2009. Irish Times Aug 2016: planted in the 18th century by the Stuarts; Department for Infrastructure proposed the ban after the 2016 storm losses and heavy traffic. Age basis: planting c.1775 per Wikipedia only (documented for the avenue, not per specimen); standing trees are survivors of that planting, so about 250 years, broad. Count is unsettled, state 'roughly 75 to 90 remain' or avoid a number; do not say 150 remain. Game of Thrones King's Road location, heavy visitor numbers. Hosts: Irish Times and Irish News fetched ok; Wikipedia fetched; wikidata API rate limited.

name: Old Homer

location.address: Kilbroney Park, Fairy Glen entrance, Shore Road, Rostrevor BT34 3BT

story:
In the summer of 2020 the council cut close to two tons off Northern Ireland's favourite tree to stop it falling over. Old Homer is a holm oak that grows at roughly 45 degrees, just inside the Fairy Glen entrance to Kilbroney Park. In 2016 it took more than half the public vote for the Woodland Trust's Northern Ireland Tree of the Year, and in 2017 it came sixth of sixteen in the European contest, with 7,101 votes.

The lean nearly finished it. In July 2020 a local councillor warned that large splits and cracks at the base meant it might not survive the next snowfall. A few weeks later the council's grounds manager, Jonathan Ellis, had the crown reduced, and the tree was declared saved, with a support underneath planned. One bough has since been propped, Wikipedia says. We have not seen a page confirming the full support went in.

It was planted about 200 years ago, the Irish News reports, by the Ross family, when this was their private estate rather than a council park. It is a little under four metres round, with bark like snakeskin. Holm oaks are evergreen, so it looks much the same in January as in June.

The last report on the tree itself that we found dates from 2020 and early 2021, so if you have walked past it lately, tell us how it is holding up. The park is free and open year round, about ten minutes' walk from Rostrevor.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the lean, roughly 45 degrees, and its snakeskin-like bark, with a propped bough. It stands just inside the Fairy Glen entrance to Kilbroney Park; our pin marks the entrance, not the trunk.
access: Free. Kilbroney Park is council-owned (Newry, Mourne and Down) and open to all, open year round from 9 am per Wikipedia; the tree is just inside the Fairy Glen pedestrian entrance, a short footpath walk from Rostrevor village. A car park is reached by the park's forest drive; no parking charge seen on a fetched page.
transport: Rostrevor village is about 10 min on foot from the Fairy Glen entrance; bus service to Rostrevor from Newry not checked.
pin_source: OSM node 728052904 'Kilbroney Park, The Fairy Glen' (54.0981385, -6.1886486), the entrance area, not the tree. Irish News and Wikipedia place the tree just inside the Fairy Glen pedestrian entrance.
recognise_facts: A holm oak leaning at roughly 45 degrees, snakeskin-like bark, just inside the Fairy Glen entrance; propped after crown work in 2020.
verify_notes: NI Tree of the Year 2016 (Woodland Trust public vote, over half the votes; Irish News 19 Dec 2016); sixth of 16 in European Tree of the Year 2017 with 7,101 votes (Wikipedia). Planted about 200 years ago by the Ross family when the land was their private estate (Irish News). Girth nearly 12 ft (3.6 m) per Irish News and Armagh I (Wikipedia says 3.7 m); 365 cm used. Condition: Armagh I 23 Jul 2020: large splits and cracks at the base, rope-like secondary growth, councillor warned it could fall; Armagh I 8 Aug 2020: council grounds manager Jonathan Ellis did a crown reduction removing close to two tons, 'saved', support underneath planned and 'soon to be installed'; Wikipedia says one bough was recently propped. Not confirmed on a seen page that the support is installed. Alive: area iNaturalist obs 2026-07-18 (weak), last tree-specific report is Aug 2020 plus Garden News Jan 2021 (search listing); flagged for no recent tree-specific life check. Other trees in park per Wikipedia: 500-year-old sessile oak, 200-year-old Turkey oak (most photographed), 200-year-old Monterey pine, 12 redwoods planted 1880 to 1890; a lead only. Ross family: unconfirmed beyond Irish News.

name: The Castlewellan Great Redwoods

location.address: Annesley Garden (walled garden and arboretum), Castlewellan Forest Park, Castlewellan BT31 9BU

story:
Northern Ireland's Forest Service book on remarkable trees calls one of these the most gigantic of all Ulster's redwoods. It stands beside formal steps near the entrance path of the Castlewellan arboretum, and directly opposite, across the path, stands another giant that the book says is nearly as tall and measures 22 feet 2 inches, about 6.75 metres, round at chest height. The text does not make clear which of the two that girth belongs to, so we give it to the pair rather than guess. No height in metres has been published.

The park's giant sequoias came from seed William Lobb brought from California in 1853 and were planted out as saplings in 1856. Nobody has written down when this pair went in, so their age here is the age of the park's sequoias in general, more than 160 years, not a date for these two. They may be younger.

The path runs between them, so you meet the pair before you meet anything else in the arboretum. That is the whole visit, and it is enough.

We found no dated report on the pair from the last few years, and our pin comes from a photographer's position in 2012, so it is close but not exact. If you see them, tell us. The park is free on foot, with a charge for cars, and the Annesley Garden is open daily from 10 am until sunset.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as two huge redwoods facing each other across the path, beside the formal steps near the arboretum's entrance path. They tower over everything around them.
access: Free on foot; vehicle access charges apply at the park (NI Forest Service, amounts on nidirect, not fetched). The walled Annesley Garden is open daily from 10.00 am to sunset, reached through the forest park (nidirect Castlewellan Forest Park page, fetched).
transport: Castlewellan village is about 1.5 km from the park entrance; Ulsterbus Newcastle to Newry services stop in Castlewellan. No rail.
pin_source: Geograph/Commons photo 'Giant Redwoods in the Castlewellan Castle Arboretum' (Eric Jones, 2012) geotagged 54.26534, -5.95243 (10 m precision, subject heading 67 degrees); consistent with the book's 'beside formal steps near the entrance path'. Not a pin on one named crown.
recognise_facts: Two huge redwoods face each other across the path beside formal steps near the entrance path of the arboretum; the pair towers over everything around it.
verify_notes: Northern Ireland's Remarkable Trees (Forest Service book, remarkabletrees.org, read via Wayback 2025-12 copy): 'the most gigantic of them all' of the Ulster redwoods is in the arboretum at Castlewellan, standing beside formal steps near the entrance path. Opposite is another giant, the Sierra Redwood, nearly as tall and measuring 22 ft 2 in (about 675 cm) at chest height; unclear from the text which one is the 22 ft 2 in tree, so girth_cm left empty. Folded as one ensemble with one place to stand. No metre height stated. Age: Castlewellan sequoias grown from William Lobb seed introduced 1853 and planted as saplings 1856 (Wikipedia, Down News); the great redwoods' own planting date not stated, so age is 'over 160 years' only as the park's sequoias, not claimed for this pair specifically. Alive: no dated post-2022 report seen for this pair; flagged. The book calls it the biggest in Ulster but gives no champion record figure; do not write a superlative beyond 'the book names it the most gigantic of Ulster's redwoods'.

name: The Castlewellan Multi-Stemmed Sequoia

location.address: Walled Annesley Garden, Castlewellan Forest Park, Castlewellan BT31 9BU

story:
This giant sequoia has nineteen trunks, a form its admirers say is rarely seen outside the wild. Instead of one column it grew a family. Its lower branches swept sideways, bowed to the ground and layered, rooting where they touched and sending up new stems, until one tree became a small grove of itself.

Its start is unusually well recorded. William Lobb brought the seed from California in 1853 for the Veitch nurseries, and this tree went into the walled garden at Castlewellan as a sapling in 1856. In 1871 the 5th Earl Annesley photographed it at fifteen years old, so there is a picture of this tree as a teenager. It is about 170 years old now.

In 2018 Northern Ireland voted it Tree of the Year, with 912 votes in the Woodland Trust contest. Plenty of trees here are bigger. This is the one whose shape is the point.

Nobody has published its girth or height, and we found no dated report since the award and the Forest Service book, so a recent photograph is welcome. Our pin is the centre of the walled Annesley Garden, not the tree, though nineteen trunks beside a path are hard to miss. The park is free on foot, with a charge for cars, and the garden opens daily from 10 am until sunset.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its 19 separate trunks and branches that sweep sideways and bow to the ground. It stands beside a path in the walled Annesley Garden; our pin marks the garden, not the tree.
access: Free on foot; vehicle access charges apply at the park (NI Forest Service, amounts on nidirect, not fetched). The walled Annesley Garden is open daily from 10.00 am to sunset, reached through the forest park (nidirect Castlewellan Forest Park page, fetched).
transport: Castlewellan village is about 1.5 km from the park entrance; Ulsterbus Newcastle to Newry services stop in Castlewellan. No rail.
pin_source: Walled garden centre (Heron Fountain area, 54.2651, -5.9506); no source gives a coordinate for this crown.
recognise_facts: A giant sequoia with 19 separate trunks; the branches sweep sideways and bow to the ground, and young climbers love it. Stands beside a path in the walled garden.
verify_notes: Northern Ireland Tree of the Year 2018 (Woodland Trust, 912 votes; Down News 17 Oct 2018 and Redwood World). Planted as a sapling in 1856 (Redwood World quoting the nomination; a photograph of it by the 5th Earl Annesley in 1871 shows it at fifteen years old) from seed brought from California by William Lobb in 1853 for Veitch Nurseries. 19 trunks, 'a form rarely seen other than in the wild'; the Remarkable Trees book describes the branches layering and forming new trees. Down News says 'over 160 years old'. Same tree as Wikipedia's 'one tree has developed 19 separate trunks'. Girth and height not published. Alive: ToY 2018 and the book; no recent dated report seen; flagged.

name: The Original Castlewellan Gold

location.address: Ornamental gardens, Castlewellan Forest Park, Castlewellan BT31 9BU

story:
Thousands of golden hedges in Northern Ireland began as cuttings from one odd seedling in these gardens. It was a mutant, a Leyland cypress with golden foliage, and the park's director, John Keown, spotted it, nurtured it and sheltered it. In 1963 it was named Cupressus macrocarpa 'Keownii', though later botanists class it as a hybrid that arose beside a Nootka cypress, not a pure Monterey cypress. Under the name Castlewellan Gold its cuttings were planted as hedges right across Ulster.

The original is young by the standards of this map. It was a seedling in the early 1960s, so it is about sixty years old at most. It is here because it is the parent of a hedge plant that many people walk past every day without knowing where it came from.

We have to be honest about two things. We do not know for certain that the original still stands. The sources that name it are older, and the most recent mention we found is a 2026 visitor guide listing it among the park's champions, which is not the same as somebody checking. And our pin marks the Heron Fountain area of the ornamental gardens, where it is said to grow, not the tree itself. Without a label it may be hard to tell from its neighbours.

If you have seen it recently, a photograph and a word would settle both questions. The park is free on foot, with a charge for cars.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its golden foliage, the parent of every Castlewellan Gold hedge. It is said to stand in the ornamental gardens near the Heron Fountain, and without a sign it may be hard to tell from its neighbours.
access: Free on foot; vehicle access charges apply at the park (NI Forest Service, amounts on nidirect, not fetched). The walled Annesley Garden is open daily from 10.00 am to sunset, reached through the forest park (nidirect Castlewellan Forest Park page, fetched).
transport: Castlewellan village is about 1.5 km from the park entrance; Ulsterbus Newcastle to Newry. No rail.
pin_source: Approximate: 'ornamental gardens' per Wikipedia; sources elsewhere say two parent trees stand in the lee of the Heron Fountain area (search snippet, unseen on a fetched page). Pin set at the Heron Fountain.
recognise_facts: A golden-foliaged cypress in the ornamental gardens, the mother of every 'Castlewellan Gold' hedge in the country; may be hard to tell from its neighbours without a sign.
verify_notes: Two sources: Wikipedia (Castlewellan Gold Leyland cypress developed in the park from a mutant, selected by park director John Keown, named Cupressus macrocarpa 'Keownii' in 1963; original specimen in the ornamental gardens) and the Remarkable Trees book (the original is the source of the thousands of cuttings planted as hedges across Ulster; spotted as a seedling, nurtured and sheltered). Hybrid, not pure macrocarpa (Conifer Society / RBG Victoria entries say it arose beside Nootka cypress). Tree is about 60-65 years old at most (seedling stage in the early 1960s); no girth. Alive now unconfirmed: no dated report; is the original still standing? Flagged, must be checked before writing. Pin not on a crown.

name: The Castlewellan Nutmeg Tree

location.address: Annesley Garden / arboretum, Castlewellan Forest Park, Castlewellan BT31 9BU

story:
Castlewellan's district council calls this the tallest California nutmeg in Britain and Ireland, one of 47 champion trees in the park's collection. The claim is undated, and the measurements we can find are old. Bean's Trees and Shrubs records it at 66 feet tall and 10.75 feet round in 1982, about 20 metres by 3.3 metres, up from 56 feet in 1976. A later record from 2000 gives a trunk diameter of 123 cm. Nobody has published a figure since, so read the crown as the council's and the numbers as forty years old.

Between 1976 and 1982 it put on ten feet in height, which is the last growth anyone recorded.

Here is the problem with visiting it. No source we have read says where in the collection it stands. Our pin is the centre of the walled Annesley Garden, and we cannot tell you which tree to look for beyond its species. Its age is not documented either.

So this is a tree for someone who knows conifers, or who asks at the park. If you find it, tell us where it stands, and a photograph of the trunk would put it properly on the map. The park is free on foot, with a charge for cars, and the garden is open daily from 10 am until sunset.
how_to_recognise: We cannot yet say which tree in the collection it is; no source gives its spot. It is said to stand in the Annesley Garden arboretum, and if you find it, tell us where.

transport: Castlewellan village is about 1.5 km from the park entrance; Ulsterbus Newcastle to Newry. No rail.

Bean's Trees and Shrubs (Trees and Shrubs Online, fetched): Castlewellan 66 x 10.75 ft (1982), i.e. about 20 m tall and 328 cm girth in 1982 (earlier 56 x 10.25 ft in 1976). name: The King Tree
story:
One of the horse chestnuts on Armagh's Mall has been called the King Tree by a neighbour since childhood. The person who named it grew up in a Georgian house across the road, and in 2019 the tree was nominated for the Woodland Trust's Northern Ireland Tree of the Year. It made the shortlist, described as a primary veteran horse chestnut.

The Mall itself is the reason it has company. The oval was laid out as a public park in the late 18th century, it is still lined with trees and surrounded by Georgian buildings, and its trees are protected. In 2020 the council scheduled works on 21 of them and removed a hollow lime at the Gaol end.

We have to be plain about the gaps. Nobody has published this tree's age, girth or planting date. Our only source is the 2019 shortlist, so the last confirmation that it stands is from that year. And no source says which trunk on the Mall it is. Our pin sits in the middle of the park, not on the tree.

That makes this a tree for somebody local. If you know which chestnut the King Tree is, or can photograph it, tell us and we will move the pin to where it belongs. In May, when the chestnuts flower, the Mall is worth the walk whichever trunk it turns out to be. It is free and open, a few minutes on foot from the bus station on Dobbin Street.
how_to_recognise: We cannot yet tell you which trunk it is, because no source places it among the horse chestnuts on the oval Mall. It stands somewhere on the Mall, framed by Georgian buildings, and a local who knows it can help us.

best_time.label: May, when white candles stand upright over the whole crown

access: Free, public park; the Mall is open ground in the centre of Armagh city.
transport: In Armagh city centre; a few minutes' walk from the bus station on Dobbin Street.
pin_source: Centre of the Mall (OSM park relation 12483402). The sources say only that the tree stands on the oval, tree-lined Mall among Georgian buildings; no coordinate for the trunk.
recognise_facts: On the oval, tree-lined Mall, surrounded by Georgian buildings. A nominator who grew up in a Georgian house across the road from it has called it the King Tree since childhood. Which trunk on the Mall it is cannot be told from sources; needs a local look.
verify_notes: Shortlisted for the Woodland Trust Northern Ireland Tree of the Year 2019, listed as 'a primary veteran horse chestnut' in Armagh, nominated by Karen Edgar for Armagh City, Banbridge and Craigavon Council (armaghi.com article read; Newsletter copy confirmed in search results but behind a Cloudflare challenge, unseen). No age, girth or planting date given anywhere seen. Alive: confirmed only as of the 2019 shortlist; no recent dated report. Armagh Council notice of Aug 2020 says 21 other protected trees on the Mall get works (so the Mall trees are protected) and a hollow lime at the Gaol end was removed. Note: the Mall was laid out as a public park c.1773/1797. The Archbishop of Armagh said in 2021 that a venerable oak planted in the Mall in the 1790s remains (lead, not placed). Single-source (shortlist press); spot unplaced.

name: The Gosford Champion Fir

location.address: Gosford Forest Park arboretum, Markethill, County Armagh BT60 1GD

story:
The record books give this fir the greatest girth of any of its species. It is a Himalayan fir, Abies spectabilis, and Northern Ireland's Forest Service book on remarkable trees puts it at 13 feet 10 inches round, about 4.2 metres, and calls it extremely tall. It is the champion of the Gosford arboretum, and at the time the book was written it was in excellent health.

That is almost everything anyone has written about it, and we should say what is missing. The book does not date the measurement, and it was published somewhere between about 2005 and 2015, so the figure may be twenty years old. It gives no height. Nobody has dated the tree. And we have only that one source, which is why it carries a flag. If the tree has fallen, we have not heard.

What the book does give is a sense of the place. The arboretum is quiet and grassy, the trees well spaced, and the fir keeps company with a group of veteran Douglas firs whose bark has gone craggy and carbuncled with age.

Our pin is the middle of the forest park, not the tree. If you find it, a photograph and a position would help the next visitor. The park is open to the public, with a charge for cars.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a well-spaced, very tall fir about 4.2 metres round in the quiet, grassy arboretum. A group of veteran Douglas firs with craggy, carbuncled bark stands near it; our pin marks the park, not the tree.
access: NI Forest Service park, open to the public; vehicle charge applies (not fetched). Check nidirect Gosford Forest Park before travelling.
transport: Markethill is about 2 km from the park entrance; Ulsterbus Armagh to Newry services call at Markethill.
pin_source: Park centroid (OSM relation 5328043). The book says only 'the arboretum'. Not a pin on the tree.
recognise_facts: Stands in the quiet, grassy arboretum, well spaced, accompanied by a group of veteran Douglas firs with craggy, carbuncled bark.
verify_notes: Single source: Northern Ireland's Remarkable Trees (Forest Service book, remarkabletrees.org, Wayback 2025-12 copy): the arboretum champion is Abies spectabilis, 'in the record books at the greatest girth for this species', 13 ft 10 in round (= 421 cm; measurement date not given, book published about 2005 to 2015) and 'extremely tall', in excellent health at the time of writing. Alive today not independently confirmed; no height figure. Register-only style source, flagged.
